title: The replica that copied the damage
outcome: The disaster recovery plan replicated storage to another region, so when a bad job corrupted a table, the replica was corrupted too.

content.bookmark: Disaster recovery protects against losing a region, not against bad data: corruption replicates. Recover bad data with time travel or backups; replicate managed tables with Deep Clone.

check.prompt: Does a disaster recovery solution protect against data corruption?
options: Yes: the secondary region always keeps a clean copy from before the error
No: corrupted data replicates; use time travel or backups
check.why: Databricks' guidance: a DR solution does not mitigate data corruption, because corrupted data replicates. Use time travel or backups for that.

check.prompt: How does Databricks recommend replicating managed table data to a DR region?
options: Rely on geo-redundant storage of the workspace's root storage
check.why: Replicate managed table data with Deep Clone, not by relying on geo-redundant storage of the workspace root storage.

options: How much data loss is tolerated
How long restoring service may take
How many regions are in use
check.why: RPO is the data loss tolerated; RTO is the time to restore. Both are business decisions.

check.prompt: What is high availability within one region?
options: A secondary workspace in another region
check.why: HA is zone redundancy inside a region; DR is a secondary workspace in another region.

caseStudy.setting: An insurer (fictional) runs its claims platform on Azure Databricks. The DR plan, written early, says "storage is geo-redundant, so data is safe in the paired region". No one has tested a restore.

events.what: A faulty release of a nightly job overwrites claim statuses in a core managed table with wrong values.
Someone suggests failing over to the DR region. The replica has the same wrong statuses: the corruption replicated overnight.
The table is recovered with RESTORE from Monday's version, which is within the retention period. The board asks whether the DR plan protects anything at all.

pipeline: Primary workspace · claims tables, nightly jobs
Storage · geo-redundant replication to the paired region
DR plan · no secondary workspace, no tested restore
tasks: Why didn't the DR plan help?

debrief.title: Why DR didn't help
text: Replication copies whatever is written, including bad writes. Databricks says it plainly: a DR solution does not mitigate data corruption.
What saved the day was time travel: RESTORE to Monday's version worked because the files were still within the retention period.

debrief.title: Two different protections
text: For bad data: time travel and RESTORE within retention, with retention set long enough for how quickly the business notices errors, and backups for longer needs.

For losing a region: a secondary workspace in another region with replicated data and configuration. Databricks recommends its managed disaster recovery, and replicating managed tables with Deep Clone rather than relying on geo-redundant root storage. Active-passive is the common pattern.

debrief.title: What the plan needs
text: RPO and RTO agreed with the business per system, not assumed by engineers.
A tested failover and a tested restore, done on a schedule. A restore also needs its downstream effects handled, since RESTORE is a data change that streams reading the table can see as new data.

takeaway: DR covers losing a region; it doesn't undo bad data.
Time travel and backups recover corruption; set retention to match.
Agree RPO and RTO with the business, and test both recoveries.
content.honesty: If you haven't designed disaster recovery for a data platform, say so, and explain the difference between DR and recovering from corruption. If you have, describe what you tested.

tasks: What should the business decide in the DR plan?
How do you know the plan works?

debrief.title: Business decisions
text: How much data loss (RPO) and downtime (RTO) each system can tolerate, and what that is worth paying for.

debrief.title: Knowing it works
text: Scheduled tests of failover and of restoring a corrupted table, with results reported.

sayIt.question: How would you set the recovery requirements for a business-critical data platform?
points: Separate losing a region from bad data.
Have the business set RPO and RTO per system.
Weigh the cost of each level of protection.
Require regular recovery tests.
Review requirements as the business changes.

tasks: How do you answer the board?
What do you put on the roadmap?

debrief.title: The board
text: The plan protects against losing a region's storage, not against bad data. Time travel recovered this incident. We will separate the two protections and test both.

debrief.title: Roadmap
text: Agreed RPO and RTO, retention settings per critical table, a secondary-region design, and a test schedule.

sayIt.question: Leadership asks whether your platform could survive a disaster. How do you answer?
points: Distinguish the scenarios: region loss, corruption, human error.
State what is protected today and what isn't.
Say when recovery was last tested.
Propose the gaps to close with costs.
Commit to regular tests.

tasks: How do you organise DR testing?

debrief.title: Testing
text: A schedule of exercises: restoring a table from history, and failing over to the secondary workspace; findings tracked as actions.

debrief.title: Ownership
text: The platform lead owns the plan; the business owns RPO and RTO; each team owns its runbooks.

sayIt.question: How do you make sure recovery plans actually work?
points: Test them on a schedule, not only on paper.
Test the realistic scenarios, including bad data.
Time the tests against RTO.
Fix what the tests reveal.
Keep the plan current as the platform changes.

tasks: What would you build for corruption recovery?
What would you build for region loss?

debrief.title: Corruption
text: Retention on critical tables long enough for errors to be found; a tested RESTORE runbook; snapshots for long-term needs.

debrief.title: Region loss
text: A secondary workspace in another region, configuration deployed to both from code, managed tables replicated with Deep Clone or Databricks' managed disaster recovery.

sayIt.question: Explain high availability and disaster recovery for Databricks.
points: HA is zone redundancy within a region.
DR is a secondary workspace in another region with replicated data and configuration.
RPO and RTO are business decisions.
Replicate managed tables with Deep Clone; Databricks offers managed disaster recovery.
DR doesn't fix corruption: use time travel and backups.
